title: The Pizza Tracker: We Were Trained to Pay for Fake Progress Bars
dek: Domino's pizza tracker started as an internal management tool, then became standard equipment in apps worldwide. It works because it turns waiting into visible work; and once companies discovered we love watching progress bars, they started faking them.
why: Medium information density, but the second half on "deliberate slowdowns" and "fake progress bars" is worth the price. Suited to listeners interested in product design and consumer psychology.
who: Product managers, designers, founders building consumer apps, and anyone who wants to understand "progress bar psychology."
skip: The first two minutes, a plea for reviews of Planet Money's book and game, can be skipped.

points.h: The 30-minute guarantee sold control, not speed
points.body: Domino's once promised delivery in 30 minutes or it was free. The guarantee made drivers speed, which led to deaths and lawsuits, and it was eventually dropped. But David Halbenstricker has a theory: the guarantee was popular not just because it was fast, but because it gave customers a sense of control. In the early 2000s Domino's commissioned a study and found that the customer's psychology after ordering a pizza is a roller coaster: the peak is at the moment of ordering, then it slides all the way down — "Where's my pizza? Did they lose my order?" However long the actual wait, what customers hate is the waiting itself.

points.h: The internal tool had to work before customers got one
points.body: Executives did not initially want to build a pizza tracker, because tracking every pizza at every store was too time-consuming and looked like a gimmick. What they were actually obsessed with was "out-the-door time." A UK franchisee put the out-the-door times of five to ten nearby stores on a single display so they would compete with each other, and handed cash bonuses to the top-ranked stores. After David's boss visited the UK, he had David replicate the system in the US. David connected every store's out-the-door time to a central system and built a real-time dashboard. The CEO said it was the thing that drove performance most in his tenure.

points.h: The tracker was a byproduct of the internal system
points.body: David and a colleague realised they already had a system tracking every pizza, so they decided to "hitch a ride" and build a customer-facing tracker. In 2006 most people didn't have smartphones; FedEx, UPS and Amazon could track packages, but on a timescale of days, not minutes. Real-time tracking of pizza progress was entirely new. The designer's interface looked like a horizontal thermometer: order, prep, bake, box, delivery — each step completed turned the next segment red. When David saw the mockup he said: "That's a hot dog. We're a pizza company, why is there a hot dog?" But executives liked it, and decided to launch before the Super Bowl.

points.h: Designers use the pizza tracker as a meeting prop
points.body: Shuya Gong was a design director at IDEO and later taught design at Harvard. Consulting for many companies in the mid-2010s, she found one of the most effective ways to open a meeting was to order a pizza on the spot, throw the tracker up on the big screen, and ask the client: "How do you feel right now?" She says you can feel the anxiety rise or fall in your body, feel the reassurance and groundedness. Then you can ask: which of those parts do you want your users to feel when they use your product? The pizza tracker became shorthand in her design circle: whenever a client involved waiting, they'd say "they need a pizza tracker."

points.h: The tracker manufactures a labor illusion
points.body: Shuya says one reason the pizza tracker caught on is that as shopping became more digital, the tracker replicated something important from the physical world — watching other people work. Online experiences lack that visibility, so people get impatient more easily. Researchers found that reminding customers there is labor behind a product makes them value it more, which they call the "labor illusion." Shuya also describes a stranger mechanism: the tracker changes our perception of time. Like walking somewhere and finding the return trip feels shorter because the route is familiar and has landmarks. The pizza tracker gives us familiar routes and landmarks — pizza being made, on the road, out for delivery — making the wait feel shorter.

points.h: Banks deliberately slow transfers to fake a wait
points.body: Working with banks and fintech companies in the mid-2010s, Shuya found their problem was the opposite of Domino's: customers weren't used to transfers being that fast. Two computers talk, confirm the amount, and the money is gone — no road to cross, no cheese to melt. But to people used to money taking a while to arrive, instant arrival "feels suspicious." So companies deliberately slow down the "money tracker," withholding real-time feedback and adding a buffer that makes you wait. Shuya says this is intentionally slowing down time, adding meaningful friction so that in the waiting you feel the seriousness and weight of the transfer. The host presses: isn't that advising lying to customers? Shuya says she prefers to understand it as "curating the experience," adding back the physicality that existed in the traditional experience, to make people comfortable.

points.h: TurboTax and Uber progress bars may be fake
points.body: TurboTax pops up an animation during filing that says "we're checking your deductions and credits." But a few years ago someone looked at the code and found the animation was identical for everyone, in every situation, and took the same amount of time. The question is: is TurboTax trying to reassure us during the terrifying ordeal of filing taxes, or using the labor illusion to make us feel a big payment is worth it? Uber is similar: the host repeatedly got updated pickup times, but the car almost always arrived later than promised. It felt like the tracker was part of a deliberate deception — to make you choose Uber over Lyft, to keep you from cancelling, to get you standing on the street early. The show contacted TurboTax and Uber; TurboTax did not respond, Uber did not arrange an interview but shared some data suggesting their pickup times are fairly accurate.

points.h: Field test: the pizza tracker is mostly real
points.body: Nick biked to a local Domino's to stake it out, while Alex ordered a half-Hawaiian, half-pepperoni pizza at home and monitored the tracker in real time. Nick ordered a pepperoni pizza in the store as cover. The tracker showed "Ivan" making the pizza, but when Nick asked the staff their name, they said "Alex." The tracker also showed a "quality check," but Nick saw no quality inspector. David had explained, though, that because Domino's uses conveyor ovens, the bake time is nearly fixed, so the tracker automatically jumps to the next step after a set time. Eventually the pizza came out, was boxed, and was driven off by Alex (aka Ivan), with Nick chasing on his bike and nearly being taken for a stalker. Alex hit "delivered" at Nick's door and the tracker updated quickly. Conclusion: the tracker is mostly accurate, but "Ivan is making it" and the "quality check" are fake.

terms.def: Reminding customers there is labor behind a product makes them value it more.
A Domino's internal metric: the time from when a pizza is ordered to when it leaves the store.
Domino's real-time order progress bar launched in 2006, widely imitated since.

quotes.text: It was a story about how an IT department of a pizza restaurant completely changed how we wait and how we feel when we wait.
We already have a system tracking every single pizza and every single Domino's. We went, ah, we can piggyback on that and do pizza tracker.

It doesn't actually take that much time for two computers to talk to each other and say, like, is this the amount of money that we're sending over? Yes, this is the amount of money we're sending over.

And so what we would do in that instance is actually slow down the pizza tracker, the money tracker. And instead of giving you a real-time reflection, we might actually give it a little bit of a buffer and make you wait.
How much are we recommending lying to your customers?

Because we've gotten so used to these kinds of apps that helped us transition to the digital world, holding our hands step by step to show us that some work was really happening, that now in our totally digital lives, we want that feeling even when it's completely disconnected from reality.
